statement: In a [projective plane](c:projective-plane), let $ABCD$ be a [complete quadrangle](c:complete-quadrangle) and $p$ a line through no vertex. Then $p$ meets the three pairs of opposite sides $(AB, CD)$, $(AC, BD)$, $(AD, BC)$ in three pairs of points that one [involution](c:projective-involution) of $p$ swaps.

hypotheses.text: The plane is the [projective plane](c:projective-plane) over a field.
The points $A, B, C, D$ form a [complete quadrangle](c:complete-quadrangle): no three of them are [collinear](c:collinear-points).
The line $p$ passes through none of $A, B, C, D$.

conclusion: Write $P, P'$ for the points where $p$ meets $AB, CD$, then $Q, Q'$ for $AC, BD$, and $R, R'$ for $AD, BC$. A projective [involution](c:projective-involution) of $p$ swaps $P \leftrightarrow P'$, $Q \leftrightarrow Q'$ and $R \leftrightarrow R'$.

proofs.name: Cross ratio by two perspectivities
proofs.slogan: Project the line $p$ from $A$ and from $B$ onto the side $CD$ to equate two cross ratios, then build the projectivity that swaps the pairs.
proofs.scope: The generic case, where $p$ avoids the three diagonal points, so the six points are distinct. A line through a diagonal point gives a fixed point of the involution; that limiting case is not proved here.

roles.why: The [cross ratio](c:cross-ratio) and the projectivity on a line over a field come from the coordinates of the [projective plane](c:projective-plane).
The sides of the [complete quadrangle](c:complete-quadrangle) meet only at vertices and diagonal points, which fixes where each perspectivity sends the six points.
Since $p$ misses $A$ and $B$, the [perspectivities](c:perspectivity) from $A$ and from $B$ are defined and keep the six points distinct.

steps.slogan: Project $p$ from $A$ onto the line $CD$.
steps.detail: Let $X = AB \cap CD$. The [perspectivity](c:perspectivity) from $A$ sends $P, P', Q, R$ to $X, P', C, D$, since $AB$ meets $CD$ at $X$, $P'$ is on $CD$, and $AC$, $AD$ meet $CD$ at $C$, $D$. It keeps the [cross ratio](c:cross-ratio), so $(P,P';Q,R) = (X,P';C,D)$.

steps.slogan: Project $p$ from $B$ onto the line $CD$.
steps.detail: The perspectivity from $B$ sends $P', P, Q', R'$ to $P', X, D, C$, since $BD$ and $BC$ meet $CD$ at $D$ and $C$ and $BA$ meets $CD$ at $X$. So $(P',P;Q',R') = (P',X;D,C)$.

steps.slogan: Swap both pairs of the cross ratio to equate the two results.
steps.detail: A cross ratio does not change when the first two points and the last two points are both swapped. Hence $(X,P';C,D) = (P',X;D,C)$, and steps 1 and 2 give $(P,P';Q,R) = (P',P;Q',R')$.

steps.slogan: Build the projectivity that swaps $P$ and $P'$ and show that it is an involution.
steps.detail: Three points determine a projectivity $\varphi$ of $p$ with $\varphi(P) = P'$, $\varphi(P') = P$, $\varphi(Q) = Q'$. Step 3 and the invariance of the cross ratio give $\varphi(R) = R'$. With $P = 0$ and $P' = \infty$ we get $\varphi(x) = k/x$, so $\varphi^2 = \mathrm{id}$, and $\varphi$ also swaps $Q', Q$ and $R', R$.

concepts.c:projective-plane: The theorem lives in the projective plane, where lines and cross ratios are defined.
concepts.c:complete-quadrangle: Its six sides give the three pairs of opposite sides that meet the line.
concepts.c:projective-involution: The swapping map of the three pairs is a projective involution.
concepts.c:collinear-points: No three vertices are collinear, so the sides are distinct lines.
concepts.c:cross-ratio: Equal cross ratios force the projectivity to match the third pair.
concepts.c:perspectivity: Projection from a vertex keeps cross ratios and moves $p$ onto a side.

source.note: The classical cross-ratio proof of Desargues' involution theorem, as in Coxeter, Projective Geometry.

statement: Let $\xi_1, \xi_2$ be [independent random variables](c:independent-random-variables) whose sum has a [Poisson distribution](c:poisson-distribution) with mean $\lambda > 0$. Then each $\xi_i$ is a Poisson variable shifted by a constant: $\xi_1 = a + \eta_1$ and $\xi_2 = -a + \eta_2$, with $\eta_i$ Poisson of mean $\lambda_i$ and $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = \lambda$.

hypotheses.text: The real random variables $\xi_1$ and $\xi_2$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables).
The sum $\xi_1 + \xi_2$ has a [Poisson distribution](c:poisson-distribution) with mean $\lambda > 0$.

conclusion: There are a real $a$ and independent Poisson variables $\eta_1, \eta_2$ with $\xi_1 = a + \eta_1$, $\xi_2 = -a + \eta_2$, and the means of $\eta_1, \eta_2$ add up to $\lambda$.

proofs.name: Lattice reduction and generating functions
proofs.slogan: Show that both variables live on a shifted copy of the nonnegative integers, then identify their generating functions as exponentials.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for real valued variables; step 1 proves that they are lattice valued. The case $\lambda = 0$ is trivial.

roles.why: Independence gives a product of probabilities in step 1 and a product of [generating functions](c:generating-function) in step 3.
The sum lives on $\mathbb{N}$ with law $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!$, which fixes the support and the product of generating functions.

steps.slogan: Show that $\xi_1$ and $\xi_2$ take values in a shifted copy of $\mathbb{N}$.
steps.detail: Take $y_0$ in the support of $\xi_2$. If $\operatorname{dist}(\xi_1 + y_0, \mathbb{N}) \ge \varepsilon$ and $|\xi_2 - y_0| < \varepsilon$, then $\xi_1 + \xi_2 \notin \mathbb{N}$. By independence $P(\operatorname{dist} \ge \varepsilon) \, P(|\xi_2 - y_0| < \varepsilon) = 0$, and the second factor is positive. So $\xi_1 + y_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ almost surely; likewise for $\xi_2$.

steps.slogan: Subtract the least values to get independent $\mathbb{N}$-valued variables with Poisson sum.
steps.detail: Each $\xi_i$ has atoms only, in a set bounded below, so it has a least atom $a$ resp. $b$. The least atom of the sum is $a + b$, and for a Poisson variable it is $0$, so $b = -a$. Then $\eta_1 = \xi_1 - a$ and $\eta_2 = \xi_2 + a$ are independent, $\mathbb{N}$-valued, and $\eta_1 + \eta_2 = \xi_1 + \xi_2$.

steps.slogan: Write the product of the two [generating functions](c:generating-function) as an exponential.
steps.detail: Let $g_i(z) = E z^{\eta_i} = \sum_n a^{(i)}_n z^n$ with coefficients $a^{(i)}_n \ge 0$ (for $z = e^{it}$ this is the [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function)). Independence gives $g_1(z) g_2(z) = e^{\lambda (z - 1)}$ for $|z| \le 1$, and $a^{(1)}_0 a^{(2)}_0 = e^{-\lambda} > 0$.

steps.slogan: Extend $g_1$ and $g_2$ to [entire functions](c:entire-function) without zeros.
steps.detail: The Cauchy product coefficients $c_n$ satisfy $c_n \ge a^{(1)}_n a^{(2)}_0$ and $c_n \ge a^{(1)}_0 a^{(2)}_n$. The product has infinite radius of convergence, and both $a^{(i)}_0 > 0$, so $g_1$ and $g_2$ have infinite radius. Then $g_1 g_2 = e^{\lambda(z-1)}$ on $\mathbb{C}$, so neither factor vanishes.

steps.slogan: Bound $g_1$ by an exponential and write $g_1 = e^{h}$ with $h$ linear.
steps.detail: For all $z$, $|g_1(z)| \le g_1(|z|) = e^{\lambda(|z| - 1)} / g_2(|z|) \le e^{\lambda |z|} / a^{(2)}_0$. Since $g_1$ has no zeros, $g_1 = e^{h}$ with $h$ entire and $\operatorname{Re} h(z) \le \lambda |z| + C$. The Borel-Carathéodory theorem gives $|h(z)| \le C'(1 + |z|)$, so $h(z) = \alpha z + \beta$.

steps.slogan: Fix $\alpha$ and $\beta$ from the signs of the coefficients and the value at $1$.
steps.detail: We have $g_1(0) = e^{\beta} = a^{(1)}_0 > 0$, so $\beta$ is real. Also $g_1'(0) = \alpha e^{\beta} \ge 0$ gives $\alpha \ge 0$, and $g_1(1) = 1$ gives $\beta = -\alpha$. So $g_1 = e^{\alpha(z-1)}$ is Poisson with mean $\alpha$, and $g_2 = e^{(\lambda - \alpha)(z-1)}$ is Poisson with mean $\lambda - \alpha$.

concepts.c:independent-random-variables: Independence splits probabilities and turns the sum into a product of generating functions.
concepts.c:poisson-distribution: The Poisson law of the sum is the datum that the factors must match.
concepts.c:generating-function: The generating function turns the convolution of laws into a product.
concepts.c:characteristic-function: On the unit circle the generating function is the characteristic function.
concepts.c:entire-function: Extending the factors to entire functions allows a growth argument.

source.note: Raikov's generating-function argument; compare E. Lukacs, Characteristic Functions, on decompositions of the Poisson law.

statement: A smooth projective [algebraic surface](c:algebraic-surface) over $\mathbb{C}$ with [irregularity](c:irregularity) $q = 0$ and second [plurigenus](c:plurigenus) $P_2 = 0$ is rational (Castelnuovo's criterion).

hypotheses.text: $S$ is a smooth projective [algebraic surface](c:algebraic-surface) over $\mathbb{C}$.
The [irregularity](c:irregularity) is $q(S) = h^1(\mathcal{O}_S) = 0$.
The second [plurigenus](c:plurigenus) is $P_2(S) = h^0(2K_S) = 0$.

conclusion: $S$ is rational: there is a [birational map](c:birational-map) $S \dashrightarrow \mathbb{P}^2$.

proofs.name: Rational curve and ruling
proofs.slogan: Pass to a minimal surface, find a smooth rational curve of nonnegative self-intersection by adjunction, and deduce that the surface is ruled over the projective line.
proofs.scope: An outline: the steps rest on Beauville's book. It proves the direction $q = P_2 = 0 \Rightarrow$ rational; the converse holds since $q$ and $P_2$ are birational invariants that vanish on $\mathbb{P}^2$.

roles.why: A smooth projective surface has a minimal model, and its geometry (Riemann-Roch, adjunction) drives every step.
The vanishing $q = 0$ gives $\chi(\mathcal{O}_S) = 1$ and forces the base of the ruling to be $\mathbb{P}^1$.
The vanishing $P_2 = 0$ makes $K_S$ not nef and makes the adjunction process stop.

steps.slogan: Replace the surface by a minimal model.
steps.detail: Contracting a $(-1)$-curve changes neither $q$, nor $P_2$, nor rationality, because the contraction is a [birational map](c:birational-map). Repeating it ends at a minimal surface with $q = P_2 = 0$. From now on $S$ is minimal.

steps.slogan: Show that the canonical class $K_S$ is not nef.
steps.detail: Since $q = 0$ and $p_g \le P_2 = 0$, we get $\chi(\mathcal{O}_S) = 1$. If $K_S$ were nef, then $h^0(-K_S) = 0$ (else $K_S = 0$ and $P_2 = 1$), and Riemann-Roch for $2K_S$ would give $h^0(2K_S) \ge 1 + K_S^2 \ge 1$. This contradicts $P_2 = 0$.

steps.slogan: Find an irreducible curve $C$ with $K_S \cdot C < 0$ and $C^2 \ge 0$.
steps.detail: Not nef gives an irreducible curve $C$ with $K_S \cdot C < 0$. If $C^2 < 0$, then adjunction $C^2 + K_S \cdot C = 2 p_a(C) - 2 \ge -2$ forces $C^2 = K_S \cdot C = -1$, so $C$ is a $(-1)$-curve, which a minimal surface does not have. So $C^2 \ge 0$.

steps.slogan: Run Castelnuovo's adjunction process on $C$ until a smooth rational curve appears.
steps.detail: Beauville passes from $C$ to the classes $C + nK_S$ while they stay effective. Because $C$ is nef and $K_S \cdot C < 0$, the process stops at an effective $D$ with $|D + K_S|$ empty. Riemann-Roch then gives $p_a(D) \le 0$, and a careful analysis yields a smooth rational curve $\Gamma$ with $\Gamma^2 \ge 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that a surface with $q = 0$ and such a curve $\Gamma$ is ruled over $\mathbb{P}^1$.
steps.detail: A smooth rational curve with $\Gamma^2 \ge 0$ moves in a family that covers $S$, so $S$ is birationally ruled over a curve $B$. Pulling back one-forms of $B$ gives $g(B) \le q(S) = 0$, so $B = \mathbb{P}^1$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that a surface birationally ruled over $\mathbb{P}^1$ is rational.
steps.detail: Such a surface is birational to $\mathbb{P}^1 \times \mathbb{P}^1$, which is birational to $\mathbb{P}^2$. So $S$ is rational, and so is the original surface, since a [birational map](c:birational-map) preserves rationality.

concepts.c:algebraic-surface: The argument works on surfaces, where adjunction and Riemann-Roch are available.
concepts.c:irregularity: The vanishing of $q$ fixes $\chi(\mathcal{O}_S)$ and the genus of the base.
concepts.c:plurigenus: The vanishing of $P_2$ rules out a nef canonical class.
concepts.c:birational-map: Contractions and the final identification with the plane are birational maps.

source.ref: A. Beauville, Complex Algebraic Surfaces, 2nd edition, London Mathematical Society Student Texts 34, Cambridge University Press, 1996, Chapter V (Castelnuovo's criterion)
source.note: The steps follow Beauville's proof: minimal model, K not nef, adjunction to a rational curve of nonnegative square, ruled over the projective line.

statement: Let $C$ be a [coalgebra](c:coalgebra) over a field $k$, and $\mathcal{M}$ its [category](c:category) of finite-dimensional [comodules](c:comodule) with the forgetful [fiber functor](c:fiber-functor) $U$ to vector spaces. Then $C$ is isomorphic, as a coalgebra, to the coend $R = \int^{M \in \mathcal{M}} U(M)^* \otimes U(M)$. So $(\mathcal{M}, U)$ determines $C$.

hypotheses.text: $C$ is a [coalgebra](c:coalgebra) over a field $k$ with comultiplication $\Delta$ and counit $\varepsilon$.
$\mathcal{M}$ is the category of finite-dimensional right [comodules](c:comodule) of $C$ and their comodule maps, and $U$ forgets the coaction.

conclusion: The map $\Phi \colon R \to C$, $[f \otimes m] \mapsto (f \otimes \mathrm{id}) \rho_M(m)$, is an isomorphism of coalgebras.

proofs.name: Coend computation
proofs.slogan: Define the map from the coend to $C$, build its inverse from finite-dimensional subcomodules, and check that both composites are identities.
proofs.scope: The Tannaka reconstruction of a coalgebra, one member of the family of reconstruction theorems. Other members (Gelfand duality, Gabriel-Rosenberg, Deligne's reconstruction of group schemes) are not proved here.

roles.why: The counit and coassociativity of $C$ give finite-dimensional subcomodules and the identity $(\varepsilon \otimes \mathrm{id})\Delta = \mathrm{id}$.
The comodule maps $\theta_f$ and the finite dimension of $M$ define $\Phi$ and give bases for the comultiplication.

steps.slogan: Show that every element of a [comodule](c:comodule) lies in a finite-dimensional subcomodule.
steps.detail: Write $\rho(m) = \sum_i m_i \otimes c_i$ with the $c_i$ linearly independent. The counit gives $m = \sum_i \varepsilon(c_i) m_i$. Coassociativity $(\rho \otimes \mathrm{id})\rho = (\mathrm{id} \otimes \Delta)\rho$ and dual functionals to the $c_i$ give $\rho(m_j) \in \operatorname{span}(m_i) \otimes C$. So $\operatorname{span}(m_i)$ is a subcomodule containing $m$.

steps.slogan: Define $\Phi$ through the comodule maps $\theta_f \colon M \to C$.
steps.detail: For $f \in M^*$ let $\theta_f(m) = (f \otimes \mathrm{id})\rho_M(m)$. Coassociativity shows that $\theta_f$ is a comodule map from $M$ to $(C, \Delta)$, and $\theta_{f g} = \theta_f g$ for comodule maps $g$. So $\Phi[f \otimes m] = \theta_f(m)$ respects the coend relations $[f g \otimes m] = [f \otimes g(m)]$.

steps.slogan: Build the inverse $\Psi \colon C \to R$ from finite-dimensional subcomodules.
steps.detail: For $x \in C$ choose a finite-dimensional subcomodule $D \ni x$ by step 1 and put $\Psi(x) = [\varepsilon|_D \otimes x]$. For $D \subseteq D'$ the inclusion $\iota$ gives $[\varepsilon|_{D'} \otimes x] = [\varepsilon|_{D'} \iota \otimes x] = [\varepsilon|_D \otimes x]$. So $\Psi$ does not depend on $D$, and comparing through $D + D'$ shows it is linear.

steps.slogan: Check that $\Phi \Psi$ is the identity of $C$.
steps.detail: We have $\Phi\Psi(x) = (\varepsilon|_D \otimes \mathrm{id})\rho(x) = (\varepsilon \otimes \mathrm{id})\Delta(x) = x$ by the counit axiom. So $\Psi$ is injective and $\Phi$ is surjective.

steps.slogan: Check that $\Psi\Phi$ is the identity of $R$ by moving $m$ into $C$.
steps.detail: Take $[f \otimes m]$ with $m \in M$. The map $\theta_f$ has finite-dimensional image $D$, a subcomodule of $C$. The coend relation for $\theta_f \colon M \to D$ gives $[f \otimes m] = [\varepsilon \theta_f \otimes m] = [\varepsilon|_D \otimes \theta_f(m)] = \Psi\Phi[f \otimes m]$, because $\varepsilon \theta_f = f$.

steps.slogan: Transport the coalgebra structure to see that $\Phi$ preserves comultiplication and counit.
steps.detail: Give $R$ the counit $[f \otimes m] \mapsto f(m)$ and the comultiplication $[f \otimes m] \mapsto \sum_i [f \otimes e_i] \otimes [e_i^* \otimes m]$ for a basis $(e_i)$ of $M$. Coassociativity of $\rho$ gives $\Delta\theta_f(m) = \sum_i \theta_f(e_i) \otimes \theta_{e_i^*}(m)$, and $\varepsilon\theta_f(m) = f(m)$. So the bijection $\Phi$ is a coalgebra map.

concepts.c:coalgebra: The object to reconstruct, with the counit and coassociativity that the proof uses.
concepts.c:comodule: Finite-dimensional comodules supply the coend and the maps $\theta_f$.
concepts.c:category: The coend is a colimit over the category of finite-dimensional comodules.
concepts.c:fiber-functor: The forgetful functor $U$ supplies the vector spaces $M^*$ and $M$ in the coend.

source.note: Standard Tannaka reconstruction for coalgebras; see A. Joyal and R. Street, An introduction to Tannaka duality and quantum groups, LNM 1488, 1991.

statement: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a [locally small](c:locally-small) category with small [limits](c:limit-category-theory). A functor $F \colon \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set}$ is [representable](c:representable-functor) iff it preserves small limits and has a solution set: a set of elements $a_i \in F(A_i)$ such that each $x \in F(X)$ equals $F(h)(a_i)$ for some $i$ and some $h \colon A_i \to X$.

hypotheses.text: The category $\mathcal{C}$ is [locally small](c:locally-small) and has all small [limits](c:limit-category-theory).
$F \colon \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set}$ is a functor.

conclusion: $F$ is [representable](c:representable-functor) if and only if $F$ preserves small limits and has a solution set.

proofs.name: Initial object of the category of elements
proofs.slogan: Turn representability into an initial object of the category of elements, and build that object by Freyd's equalizer argument.
proofs.scope: Both directions. The dual statement for contravariant functors is the same proof in the opposite category.

roles.why: Small limits in $\mathcal{C}$ give limits in the category of elements, and local smallness makes the endomorphisms of $W$ a set.
The functor $F$ defines the category of elements and its universal elements.

steps.slogan: Show that a representable functor preserves limits and has a solution set.
steps.detail: If $F \cong \operatorname{Hom}(A, -)$, then $F$ preserves every limit, since $\operatorname{Hom}(A, -)$ does. The single element $\mathrm{id}_A \in F(A)$ is a solution set: each $x \in F(X) = \operatorname{Hom}(A, X)$ equals $F(x)(\mathrm{id}_A)$.

steps.slogan: Form the category of elements and identify representing objects with its [initial objects](c:initial-object).
steps.detail: Objects of $\mathrm{El}(F)$ are pairs $(X, x)$ with $x \in F(X)$, and arrows $(X, x) \to (Y, y)$ are maps $h$ with $F(h)(x) = y$. By the Yoneda lemma an initial object $(A, a)$ gives the natural isomorphism $\operatorname{Hom}(A, -) \to F$, $h \mapsto F(h)(a)$, and conversely.

steps.slogan: Show that $\mathrm{El}(F)$ has all small [limits](c:limit-category-theory) because $F$ preserves them.
steps.detail: The forgetful functor $\mathrm{El}(F) \to \mathcal{C}$ creates limits. A limit of $(X_j, x_j)$ is $\lim X_j$ with the element of $F(\lim X_j) = \lim F(X_j)$ given by the compatible family $(x_j)$. The category $\mathrm{El}(F)$ is locally small.

steps.slogan: Turn the solution set into a [weakly initial](c:weakly-initial-object) object by taking a product.
steps.detail: The pairs $(A_i, a_i)$ are objects of $\mathrm{El}(F)$, and every object receives an arrow from one of them. The product $W = \prod_i (A_i, a_i)$ exists by step 3, and every object receives an arrow from $W$.

steps.slogan: Take the joint [equalizer](c:equalizer) of all endomorphisms of $W$.
steps.detail: Let $e \colon E \to W$ equalize all endomorphisms of $W$ in $\mathrm{El}(F)$; this is a limit over a set of arrows, so it exists by step 3. Every object $Y$ receives an arrow $E \to W \to Y$.

steps.slogan: Show that $E$ has only one arrow to each object.
steps.detail: Let $u, v \colon E \to Y$ and let $e'$ equalize them, with $s \colon W \to E'$ any arrow. Then $e e' s$ is an endomorphism of $W$, so $e e' s e = e$, so $e' s e = \mathrm{id}_E$ and $u = v$. This is Freyd's argument for the adjoint functor theorem.

steps.slogan: Read the representing object off the initial object.
steps.detail: By step 2 an initial object $(A, a)$ of $\mathrm{El}(F)$ gives $F \cong \operatorname{Hom}(A, -)$. So $F$ is representable, and step 1 gives the other direction.

concepts.c:locally-small: Local smallness makes the endomorphisms of $W$ a set, so their equalizer exists.
concepts.c:limit-category-theory: Limits in $\mathcal{C}$ and their preservation by $F$ build limits in $\mathrm{El}(F)$.
concepts.c:representable-functor: Representability is the property the theorem characterizes.
concepts.c:initial-object: A representing object is the same as an initial object of $\mathrm{El}(F)$.
concepts.c:weakly-initial-object: The solution set gives a weakly initial family, which a product makes one object.
concepts.c:equalizer: The equalizer of all endomorphisms cuts the weakly initial object down to an initial one.

source.note: Freyd's adjoint functor theorem argument applied to the category of elements; see Mac Lane, Categories for the Working Mathematician, Chapter V.

statement: Let $f \colon X \to Y$ be a smooth map of closed manifolds such that $T_f = TX - f^*TY$ has a spin$^c$ structure with first Chern class $c$. This [K-orientation](c:k-orientation) defines $f_! \colon K(X) \to K(Y)$ in [topological K-theory](c:topological-k-theory). Then $\mathrm{ch}(f_! x) = f_*\bigl(\mathrm{ch}(x)\, e^{c/2} \hat{A}(T_f)\bigr)$ in $H^*(Y; \mathbb{Q})$ for every $x \in K(X)$.

hypotheses.text: $f \colon X \to Y$ is a smooth map between closed manifolds.
The virtual bundle $T_f = TX - f^*TY$ carries a spin$^c$ structure with first Chern class $c$, so $f$ is [K-oriented](c:k-orientation).

conclusion: The [Chern character](c:chern-character) of the [Gysin](c:gysin-map) image satisfies $\mathrm{ch}(f_! x) = f_*(\mathrm{ch}(x)\, e^{c/2} \hat{A}(T_f))$ for all $x \in K(X)$.

proofs.name: Thom isomorphisms and Bott periodicity
proofs.slogan: Factor the map as an embedding followed by a projection, compare the Thom classes in K-theory and cohomology, and treat the projection by Bott periodicity.
proofs.scope: An outline of the Atiyah-Hirzebruch argument for K-oriented maps; it is the differentiable analogue of Grothendieck's Riemann-Roch theorem. Other versions of the family (almost complex, spin) are special cases.

roles.why: A smooth map of closed manifolds factors as an embedding into a product with a sphere, followed by a projection.
The spin$^c$ structure gives the K-theory Thom class of the normal bundle and the class $e^{c/2}\hat{A}$.

steps.slogan: Factor $f$ as an embedding $i$ into $Y \times S^{2n}$ followed by the projection.
steps.detail: Embed $X$ in $S^{2n}$ and put $i(x) = (f(x), j(x))$. The sphere has trivial stable tangent bundle, so $T_f = T_i$ stably and the K-orientation of $f$ is one of the normal bundle $\nu$ of $i$. Then $f_! = \mathrm{pr}_! \, i_!$ and $f_* = \mathrm{pr}_* \, i_*$.

steps.slogan: Define the Gysin map $i_!$ by the K-theory Thom isomorphism of $\nu$.
steps.detail: The spin$^c$ structure gives a K-theory Thom class $U_K$ (Bott; Atiyah-Bott-Shapiro). Then $i_! x$ is the extension by zero of $x \cdot U_K \in K(\nu)$ over a tubular neighborhood. The cohomology Gysin map $i_*$ uses the Thom class $U_H$ in the same way.

steps.slogan: Compare the Chern character of $U_K$ with $U_H$ using the splitting principle.
steps.detail: For a complex bundle the [Todd class](c:todd-class) appears: $\mathrm{ch}(U_K) = U_H \cdot \mathrm{Td}(\nu)^{-1}$, by a check on line bundles. The spin$^c$ case is the same computation with $e^{c/2}\hat{A}$, giving $\mathrm{ch}(U_K) = U_H \cdot e^{c/2} \hat{A}(T_i)$. Hence $\mathrm{ch}(i_! x) = i_*(\mathrm{ch}(x)\, e^{c/2}\hat{A}(T_i))$.

steps.slogan: Treat the projection $Y \times S^{2n} \to Y$ by Bott periodicity.
steps.detail: Bott periodicity gives $K(Y \times S^{2n}) = K(Y) \oplus K(Y)\beta$, and $\mathrm{pr}_!$ takes the coefficient of $\beta$. The class $\mathrm{ch}(\beta)$ generates $H^{2n}(S^{2n}; \mathbb{Z})$, and $\mathrm{pr}_*$ integrates over the sphere. So $\mathrm{ch}(\mathrm{pr}_! z) = \mathrm{pr}_*\mathrm{ch}(z)$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two stages to get the formula for $f$.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give $\mathrm{ch}(f_! x) = \mathrm{pr}_*\mathrm{ch}(i_! x) = \mathrm{pr}_* i_*(\mathrm{ch}(x)\, e^{c/2}\hat{A}(T_i)) = f_*(\mathrm{ch}(x)\, e^{c/2}\hat{A}(T_f))$, since $T_i = T_f$ stably.

concepts.c:k-orientation: A K-orientation is what lets $f_!$ exist on K-theory.
concepts.c:topological-k-theory: The group $K(X)$ is where the Gysin map $f_!$ acts.
concepts.c:chern-character: The Chern character carries K-theory classes to rational cohomology.
concepts.c:gysin-map: The Gysin map $f_!$ is the pushforward that the formula describes.
concepts.c:todd-class: The Todd class is the correction factor in the complex case.

source.ref: M. F. Atiyah and F. Hirzebruch, Riemann-Roch theorems for differentiable manifolds, Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 65 (1959), 276-281
source.note: The paper announces the theorem with a proof sketch; the K-theory Thom isomorphism for spin^c bundles is due to Atiyah, Bott and Shapiro (1964).

statement: For standard [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$ on $[0,1]$, the laws $\mu_\varepsilon$ of $\sqrt{\varepsilon}\, B$ in $C_0[0,1]$ satisfy a [large deviation principle](c:large-deviation-principle) as $\varepsilon \to 0$, with speed $\varepsilon$ and good rate function $I(\omega) = \tfrac12 \int_0^1 \dot\omega^2\,dt$ on the [Cameron-Martin space](c:cameron-martin-space), and $I = \infty$ elsewhere.

hypotheses.text: $B$ is a standard [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) on $[0,1]$, and $C_0[0,1]$ carries the supremum norm.

conclusion: For closed $F$, $\limsup \varepsilon \log \mu_\varepsilon(F) \le -\inf_F I$; for open $G$, $\liminf \varepsilon \log \mu_\varepsilon(G) \ge -\inf_G I$; and the sets $\{I \le a\}$ are compact.

proofs.name: Piecewise linear approximation
proofs.slogan: Approximate Brownian paths by piecewise linear paths, use the finite-dimensional Gaussian large deviation principle, and pass to the limit with exponentially good approximations.
proofs.scope: An outline: the steps rest on Dembo and Zeitouni, Section 5.2, with Cramér's theorem and the contraction principle. The Freidlin-Wentzell theorem generalizes the result to diffusions.

roles.why: Independent Gaussian increments give the finite-dimensional principle, and the reflection principle gives the exponential tail bound.

steps.slogan: Interpolate the path linearly on the grid of mesh $1/m$.
steps.detail: Let $\omega^{(m)}$ be the piecewise linear path that equals $\omega$ at the points $j/m$. The map $\omega \mapsto \omega^{(m)}$ is continuous on $C_0[0,1]$, and its image is the $m$-dimensional space $\mathcal{L}_m$ of paths that are linear on each grid interval.

steps.slogan: Prove the large deviation principle for the Gaussian vector of increments.
steps.detail: The increments $\sqrt{\varepsilon}(B_{j/m} - B_{(j-1)/m})$ are independent $N(0, \varepsilon/m)$. Cramér's theorem, or a direct Gaussian computation, gives a [large deviation principle](c:large-deviation-principle) in $\mathbb{R}^m$ with the good rate $\frac{m}{2}\sum_j \Delta_j^2$.

steps.slogan: Transfer the principle to piecewise linear paths by the contraction principle.
steps.detail: The map from increments to the path in $\mathcal{L}_m$ is linear, hence continuous. The contraction principle gives a principle for $\sqrt{\varepsilon} B^{(m)}$ with rate $I_m(\omega) = \frac12\int_0^1 \dot\omega^2\,dt$ on $\mathcal{L}_m$ and $\infty$ elsewhere.

steps.slogan: Show that the interpolations are exponentially good approximations.
steps.detail: On each grid interval $|B_s - B^{(m)}_s| \le 2\sup|B_s - B_{(j-1)/m}|$. The reflection principle gives $P(\|\sqrt{\varepsilon}(B - B^{(m)})\| > \delta) \le 4m\, e^{-m\delta^2/(8\varepsilon)}$. So $\limsup_{\varepsilon \to 0}\varepsilon \log P(\cdots) \le -m\delta^2/8$, which tends to $-\infty$ as $m \to \infty$.

steps.slogan: Pass to $m \to \infty$ and identify the good rate function.
steps.detail: The theorem on exponentially good approximations (Dembo-Zeitouni, Section 4.2) gives a principle with a good rate function that equals $\frac12 \int_0^1 \dot\omega^2\,dt$ on the [Cameron-Martin space](c:cameron-martin-space) and $\infty$ elsewhere. On $\{I \le a\}$ the bound $|\omega(t) - \omega(s)| \le \sqrt{2a|t-s|}$ and Arzelà-Ascoli give compactness.

concepts.c:brownian-motion: Brownian motion is the process whose scaled laws satisfy the principle.
concepts.c:large-deviation-principle: The principle is what is proved first for vectors and then for paths.
concepts.c:cameron-martin-space: The finite-energy paths form the set where the rate function is finite.

source.ref: A. Dembo and O. Zeitouni, Large Deviations Techniques and Applications, 2nd edition, Springer, 1998, Section 5.2 (Theorem 5.2.3, Schilder's theorem)
source.note: The steps follow Dembo and Zeitouni: finite-dimensional principle, contraction, exponentially good approximation. Original: M. Schilder, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 125 (1966), 63-85.

statement: Every language in [BPP](c:bpp) lies in $\Sigma_2^p \cap \Pi_2^p$, the second level of the [polynomial hierarchy](c:polynomial-hierarchy).

hypotheses.text: The language $L$ is decided by a probabilistic polynomial-time machine that errs with probability at most $1/3$ on every input.

conclusion: The language $L$ lies in $\Sigma_2^p$ and in $\Pi_2^p$.

proofs.name: Covering by XOR shifts (Lautemann)
proofs.slogan: Amplify the error below $2^{-n}$, then cover the random strings by a few XOR shifts of the accepting set.
proofs.scope: The class $\Sigma_2^p$ for inputs of length $n$ above a fixed constant, with shorter inputs answered by a table. The class $\Pi_2^p$ follows because BPP is closed under complement.

roles.why: The machine with bounded error gives the accepting sets $A_x$ whose sizes are close to $2^m$ or close to $0$.

steps.slogan: [Amplify](c:probabilistic-amplification) the success probability so that the error is below $2^{-n}$.
steps.detail: Run the machine $O(n)$ times on independent random strings and take the majority vote. The Chernoff bound gives error at most $2^{-n}$ with $m = \mathrm{poly}(n)$ random bits. Let $A_x \subseteq \{0,1\}^m$ be the random strings on which the new machine accepts $x$.

steps.slogan: Show that for $x \in L$ some $m$ shifts of $A_x$ cover every string.
steps.detail: Pick $t_1, \dots, t_m \in \{0,1\}^m$ at random. For a fixed $r$, each $r \oplus t_i$ is uniform and misses $A_x$ with probability at most $2^{-n}$, so all $m$ of them miss with probability at most $2^{-nm}$. The union bound over the $2^m$ strings $r$ gives failure probability at most $2^{m - nm} < 1$ for $n \ge 2$.

steps.slogan: Show that for $x \notin L$ no $m$ shifts of $A_x$ cover every string.
steps.detail: Here $|A_x| \le 2^{-n} 2^m$. So $\bigcup_i (A_x \oplus t_i)$ has at most $m 2^{-n} 2^m < 2^m$ strings once $2^n > m$, which holds for large $n$ because $m$ is a polynomial in $n$. So some $r$ is not covered.

steps.slogan: Write membership as an $\exists\forall$ statement with a polynomial-time matrix.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give: $x \in L$ iff there are $t_1, \dots, t_m$ such that for all $r$, some $M(x, r \oplus t_i)$ accepts. The matrix is checked in polynomial time, so $L \in \Sigma_2^p$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the complement to place $L$ in $\Pi_2^p$.
steps.detail: BPP is closed under complement, since the machine can swap accept and reject. So the complement of $L$ is in $\Sigma_2^p$ by step 4, and $L \in \Pi_2^p$.

concepts.c:bpp: The hypothesis puts $L$ in BPP, and the theorem bounds BPP.
concepts.c:polynomial-hierarchy: The levels $\Sigma_2^p$ and $\Pi_2^p$ are the target of the containment.
concepts.c:probabilistic-amplification: Amplification makes the error small enough for the union bound.

source.note: Lautemann's proof: C. Lautemann, BPP and the polynomial hierarchy, Information Processing Letters 17 (1983), 215-217.

statement: Let $X$ be a real random variable with $E X = 0$ and $E X^2 < \infty$, and let $W$ be a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion). Then there is a [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $\tau$, for the filtration of $W$ enlarged by an independent random variable, such that $W_\tau$ has the law of $X$ and $E \tau = E X^2$.

hypotheses.text: The variable $X$ has mean $E X = 0$.
The variable $X$ has finite variance $E X^2 < \infty$.
$W$ is a standard [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion).

conclusion: The variable $W_\tau$ has the same law as $X$, and $E \tau = E X^2$.

proofs.name: Randomized exit interval
proofs.slogan: Choose a random interval around zero so that the exit point of Brownian motion has the law of $X$, using optional stopping for the exit from a two-point interval.
proofs.scope: Skorokhod's first embedding theorem for one variable, with an independent randomization at time $0$; the randomness can be drawn from $W$ itself, which is not shown here. The embedding of a whole martingale or random walk is not proved.

roles.why: The mean zero makes the positive and negative parts of $X$ have equal mass $c$, which normalizes the law of $(U, V)$.
Finite variance makes $E\tau = E X^2$ finite.
Brownian motion supplies the [martingales](c:martingale) $W_t$ and $W_t^2 - t$ that give the exit law and the mean exit time.

steps.slogan: Draw a random interval $(U, V)$ around zero from the law $\mu$ of $X$.
steps.detail: Let $c = \int_0^\infty x\,\mu(dx) = \int_{-\infty}^0 (-x)\,\mu(dx)$, equal because $E X = 0$. If $c = 0$, then $X = 0$ and $\tau = 0$. Otherwise let $(U, V)$ be independent of $W$ with $P(U = V = 0) = \mu\{0\}$ and, on $\{U < 0 < V\}$, density $(v - u)/c$ with respect to $\mu(du)\,\mu(dv)$; its total mass is $\mu(-\infty,0) + \mu(0,\infty)$.

steps.slogan: Stop $W$ at its first exit from $(U, V)$.
steps.detail: Let $\tau = \inf\{t : W_t \notin (U, V)\}$ and $\mathcal{F}_t = \sigma(U, V, W_s : s \le t)$. Then $W$ is a Brownian motion for $\mathcal{F}_t$, so $\tau$ is a [stopping time](c:stopping-time). It is finite almost surely, because the interval is bounded, and $W_\tau \in \{U, V\}$.

steps.slogan: Compute the exit law given $(U, V)$ by optional stopping.
steps.detail: Given $(U, V) = (u, v)$ the stopped [martingale](c:martingale) $W_{t \wedge \tau}$ is bounded. Optional sampling gives $0 = u\,P(W_\tau = u) + v\,P(W_\tau = v)$, so $P(W_\tau = v \mid U, V) = -U/(V - U)$ and $P(W_\tau = U \mid U, V) = V/(V - U)$.

steps.slogan: Integrate over $(U, V)$ to show that $W_\tau$ has the law $\mu$.
steps.detail: For $v > 0$, $P(W_\tau \in dv) = \int_u \frac{-u}{v - u}\cdot\frac{v - u}{c}\,\mu(du)\,\mu(dv) = \mu(dv)$, because $\int (-u)\,\mu(du) = c$. The case $u < 0$ is symmetric, and $\{0\}$ has mass $\mu\{0\}$.

steps.slogan: Compute $E \tau$ with the martingale $W_t^2 - t$.
steps.detail: Given $(U, V)$, optional stopping and monotone convergence give $E[\tau \mid U, V] = E[W_\tau^2 \mid U, V] = -UV$. Hence $E\tau = \frac1c \iint (-u) v (v - u)\,\mu(du)\,\mu(dv) = \int v^2\,\mu(dv) + \int u^2\,\mu(du) = E X^2$.

steps.slogan: Combine the exit law and the mean exit time.
steps.detail: Steps 4 and 5 give $W_\tau \sim X$ and $E\tau = E X^2 < \infty$. So $\tau$ is a stopping time of the enlarged filtration with both properties.

concepts.c:brownian-motion: Brownian motion is the process that is stopped at the random exit time.
concepts.c:stopping-time: The exit time is a stopping time, so optional sampling applies.
concepts.c:martingale: The processes $W_t$ and $W_t^2 - t$ are martingales that give exit law and mean.

source.note: Skorokhod's randomized embedding, as in Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Section 8.1.

statement: Let $S$ be a finite set of points in the Euclidean plane that are not all [collinear](c:collinear-points). Then some line passes through exactly two points of $S$, an [ordinary line](c:ordinary-line).

hypotheses.text: $S$ is a finite set of points of the Euclidean plane.
The points of $S$ are not all [collinear](c:collinear-points).

proofs.name: Kelly's least distance
proofs.slogan: Take the point and line with the least positive distance and show that this line is ordinary.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. A set that is not collinear has at least three points, so a line through two of them that misses a third exists.

roles.why: Finitely many pairs of a point and a line give a least positive distance.
A point off a line through two points of $S$ exists, so the set of pairs is nonempty.

steps.slogan: Choose the pair of a point and a line with the least positive distance.
steps.detail: Consider pairs $(P, \ell)$ with $P \in S$ and $\ell$ a line through at least two points of $S$ with $P \notin \ell$. Some pair exists since $S$ is not collinear, and there are finitely many pairs. Take one with $d(P, \ell)$ least.

steps.slogan: Assume that $\ell$ holds three points of $S$ and drop the perpendicular from $P$.
steps.detail: Suppose $\ell$ holds at least three points of $S$. Let $F$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $\ell$. The point $F$ splits $\ell$ into two closed rays, so two of the three points, $B$ and $C$, lie on one ray with $|FB| < |FC|$.

steps.slogan: Show that $B$ is closer to the line $PC$ than $P$ is to $\ell$.
steps.detail: Let $\theta$ be the angle between $\ell$ and $PC$ at $C$. Then $d(P, \ell) = |PC| \sin\theta$ and $d(B, PC) = |BC| \sin\theta$. Since $B$ lies between $F$ and $C$ or equals $F$, $|BC| \le |FC| < |PC|$. So $0 < d(B, PC) < d(P, \ell)$, where $d(B, PC) > 0$ because $PC$ meets $\ell$ only at $C$.

steps.slogan: Contradict the minimality of the pair.
steps.detail: The line $PC$ holds the two points $P$ and $C$ of $S$ and misses $B \in S$. So $(B, PC)$ is a pair of step 1 with smaller distance, against the choice. Hence $\ell$ holds exactly two points of $S$.

concepts.c:collinear-points: Non-collinearity gives a point off every line through two points.
concepts.c:ordinary-line: The line found by minimization holds exactly two points of the set.

source.note: Kelly's proof, in H. S. M. Coxeter, A problem of collinear points, American Mathematical Monthly 55 (1948), and in Aigner and Ziegler, Proofs from THE BOOK.

statement: Let $A$ be an [affinoid algebra](c:affinoid-algebra) over a complete non-archimedean field $k$, $X = \mathrm{Sp}(A)$ the [affinoid space](c:affinoid-space), and $\mathcal{U}$ a finite covering of $X$ by rational subdomains. Then the augmented [Čech](c:cech-cohomology) complex of the structure sheaf for $\mathcal{U}$ is exact.

hypotheses.text: $X = \mathrm{Sp}(A)$ for an [affinoid algebra](c:affinoid-algebra) $A$ over a complete non-archimedean field $k$.
$\mathcal{U} = \{U_i\}$ is a finite covering of $X$ by rational subdomains.

conclusion: The complex $0 \to A \to \prod_i \mathcal{O}(U_i) \to \prod_{i<j} \mathcal{O}(U_{ij}) \to \cdots$ is exact, so $\check{H}^0 = A$ and $\check{H}^q = 0$ for $q > 0$.

proofs.name: From one-function Laurent coverings
proofs.slogan: Prove exactness for the covering by $\{|f| \le 1\}$ and $\{|f| \ge 1\}$, then reach every finite rational covering by iteration and refinement.
proofs.scope: An outline: the steps follow Tate and Bosch-Güntzer-Remmert, whose norm estimates are cited. It treats finite coverings by rational subdomains; general affinoid coverings reduce to these by the Gerritzen-Grauert theorem.

roles.why: The algebras $A\langle f\rangle$ are Banach algebras over a complete field, which allows norm estimates and the open mapping theorem.
A finite rational covering is refined by iterated Laurent coverings, and a double complex transfers exactness to it.

steps.slogan: Write the Čech complex of the covering $\{X(f), X(f^{-1})\}$ for $f \in A$.
steps.detail: The sets $X(f) = \{|f| \le 1\}$ and $X(f^{-1}) = \{|f| \ge 1\}$ cover $X$ and meet in $X(f, f^{-1})$. The complex is $0 \to A \to A\langle f \rangle \oplus A\langle f^{-1} \rangle \to A\langle f, f^{-1} \rangle \to 0$, and exactness is the claim for this covering.

steps.slogan: Split every element of $A\langle f, f^{-1}\rangle$ into a part on each piece.
steps.detail: Every $g \in A\langle f, f^{-1}\rangle$ is a series $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a_n f^n$ with $a_n \in A$ and $a_n \to 0$ as $|n| \to \infty$. Collecting $n \ge 0$ and $n < 0$ gives $g = g_+ + g_-$ with $g_+ \in A\langle f\rangle$ and $g_- \in A\langle f^{-1}\rangle$. So the last map is onto.

steps.slogan: Show exactness on the left and in the middle with norm estimates in [Banach algebras](c:banach-algebra).
steps.detail: Tate and Bosch-Güntzer-Remmert prove this with norm estimates in $A\langle f\rangle$, $A\langle f^{-1}\rangle$ and $A\langle f, f^{-1}\rangle$. They use that these are quotients of Tate algebras and that surjective maps of Banach modules are open. The result is that $A$ is the kernel and that $A$ maps injectively.

steps.slogan: Iterate to get exactness for Laurent coverings by $f_1, \dots, f_n$.
steps.detail: The Laurent covering by the sets $X(f_1^{\pm 1}, \dots, f_n^{\pm 1})$ arises by covering $X$ with the pair for $f_1$, then each piece with the pair for $f_2$, and so on. Each stage is a one-function covering, exact by step 3, and a double complex argument gives exactness for the composite.

steps.slogan: Refine a finite rational covering by Laurent coverings and compare by a double complex.
steps.detail: Tate shows that a finite covering by rational subdomains has a refinement built from Laurent coverings. The Čech complexes of the refinement restricted to each intersection are exact by step 4. A double complex comparison then makes the complex of $\mathcal{U}$ exact.

concepts.c:affinoid-algebra: The ring $A$ and its localizations carry the Banach norms used in the proof.
concepts.c:affinoid-space: The space $X = \mathrm{Sp}(A)$ is the space that the rational subdomains cover.
concepts.c:cech-cohomology: Exactness of the augmented Čech complex is the content of the theorem.
concepts.c:banach-algebra: Norm estimates and the open mapping theorem work in these Banach algebras.

source.ref: J. Tate, Rigid analytic spaces, Inventiones Mathematicae 12 (1971), 257-289; see also S. Bosch, U. Güntzer and R. Remmert, Non-Archimedean Analysis, Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften 261, Springer, 1984, Chapter 8
source.note: The steps follow the reduction of Tate's proof: one-function Laurent covering, iteration, refinement and double complex.

statement: Every continuous map of a nonempty [compact convex set](c:compact-convex-set) $K$ in a Hausdorff [locally convex space](c:locally-convex-space) into itself has a [fixed point](c:fixed-point).

hypotheses.text: $E$ is a Hausdorff [locally convex space](c:locally-convex-space).
$K \subseteq E$ is nonempty, compact and convex.
$f \colon K \to K$ is continuous.

conclusion: There is a point $y \in K$ with $f(y) = y$.

proofs.name: Schauder projections and Brouwer
proofs.slogan: Approximate $f$ on finite-dimensional compact convex sets by Schauder projections, apply Brouwer's theorem there, and take a limit point of the approximate fixed points.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The empty set has no fixed point, so $K \ne \emptyset$ is needed.

roles.why: Local convexity gives convex neighborhoods of $0$ with continuous Minkowski functionals, and the Hausdorff property forces the limit to be fixed.
Compactness gives finite covers and a convergent subnet, and convexity keeps the projections inside $K$.
Continuity makes $p_V \circ f$ continuous for Brouwer's theorem and lets the subnet pass to the limit.

steps.slogan: Fix a convex balanced open neighborhood $V$ of $0$ and cover $K$ by finitely many translates.
steps.detail: Compactness of $K$ gives $K \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^n (x_i + V)$ with $x_i \in K$. The [convex hull](c:convex-hull) $C_V = \operatorname{conv}\{x_1, \dots, x_n\}$ lies in $K$ by convexity and is a compact convex subset of a finite-dimensional subspace.

steps.slogan: Build the Schauder projection $p_V \colon K \to C_V$ with $p_V(x) - x \in V$.
steps.detail: Let $\rho$ be the Minkowski functional of $V$, so $V = \{\rho < 1\}$. Put $\varphi_i(x) = \max(0, 1 - \rho(x - x_i))$, positive exactly when $x \in x_i + V$, and $p_V(x) = \sum_i \varphi_i(x) x_i / \sum_j \varphi_j(x)$. The map $p_V$ is continuous, and $p_V(x) - x$ is a convex combination of vectors $x_i - x \in V$, so it lies in $V$.

steps.slogan: Apply Brouwer's theorem to $p_V \circ f$ on $C_V$.
steps.detail: The map $p_V \circ f$ is a continuous self-map of $C_V$, which is homeomorphic to a compact convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$. So there is $y_V \in C_V$ with $p_V(f(y_V)) = y_V$, and then $f(y_V) - y_V \in V$.

steps.slogan: Take a convergent subnet of the points $y_V$ as $V$ shrinks.
steps.detail: Direct the neighborhoods $V$ by reverse inclusion. The net $(y_V)$ lies in the compact set $K$, so a subnet converges to some $y \in K$.

steps.slogan: Show that $f(y) - y$ lies in every neighborhood of $0$.
steps.detail: Along the subnet, $f(y_V) - y_V \to f(y) - y$ by continuity of $f$, and $f(y_V) - y_V \in V$. For a convex balanced open $W$, eventually $V \subseteq W$, so $f(y) - y \in \overline{W}$. In a Hausdorff space such closures meet in $\{0\}$, so $f(y) = y$.

concepts.c:compact-convex-set: Compactness and convexity of $K$ give finite covers and keep projections in $K$.
concepts.c:locally-convex-space: Convex neighborhoods of $0$ supply the Minkowski functionals for the projections.
concepts.c:fixed-point: The theorem produces a fixed point as a limit of approximate ones.
concepts.c:convex-hull: The hull of the finitely many centers is the finite-dimensional set where Brouwer applies.

source.note: The Schauder-projection argument; the theorem is due to A. Tychonoff, Ein Fixpunktsatz, Mathematische Annalen 111 (1935).

statement: Let $f$ and $g$ be locally integrable functions on $\mathbb{R}$ that vanish on $(-\infty, 0)$. Then the [convolution](c:convolution) $f * g$ satisfies $\inf \operatorname{supp}(f * g) = \inf \operatorname{supp} f + \inf \operatorname{supp} g$, where the [support](c:support) is the essential support and $\inf \emptyset = +\infty$.

hypotheses.text: $f$ and $g$ are locally integrable on $\mathbb{R}$.
$f$ and $g$ vanish on $(-\infty, 0)$, so $(f * g)(x) = \int_0^x f(t) g(x - t)\,dt$.

proofs.name: Growth of Fourier-Laplace transforms
proofs.slogan: Reduce to compact supports, read the left end of the support from the growth of the transform along the imaginary axis, and add the growth rates of the factors.
proofs.scope: An outline: the steps follow the Lions-Hörmander proof for compactly supported distributions, whose entire-function lemmas are cited. If $f = 0$ or $g = 0$, both sides are $+\infty$.

roles.why: After truncation, integrability makes the transforms entire functions of exponential type that are bounded on the real axis.
Supports in $[0, \infty)$ make the convolution a finite integral and let the left ends of the supports add.

steps.slogan: Truncate $f$ and $g$ to compactly supported functions.
steps.detail: Let $a = \inf\operatorname{supp} f$ and $b = \inf\operatorname{supp} g$, both finite. For $R > a + b$ put $f_R = f \mathbf{1}_{[0,R]}$ and $g_R = g\mathbf{1}_{[0,R]}$. Then $f_R * g_R = f * g$ on $[0, R]$, and $\inf\operatorname{supp} f_R = a$, $\inf\operatorname{supp} g_R = b$. Since $f * g = 0$ below $a + b$, it suffices that $f * g$ is not zero on $[0, a + b + \varepsilon]$, and $f_R, g_R$ decide this.

steps.slogan: Pass to the [Fourier-Laplace transforms](c:fourier-laplace-transform), which are entire of exponential type.
steps.detail: For $f$ in $L^1$ with support in $[0, A]$ put $F(\zeta) = \int_0^A f(t) e^{-i t \zeta}\,dt$. By the Paley-Wiener-Schwartz theorem $F$ is an [entire function](c:entire-function) of [exponential type](c:function-of-exponential-type), bounded on the real axis. The same holds for $G$, and $F G$ is the transform of $f * g$.

steps.slogan: Read the left end of the support from the growth of $F$ along the imaginary axis.
steps.detail: The growth rate $h_F = \limsup_{y \to \infty} y^{-1}\log|F(-iy)|$ is at most $-\inf\operatorname{supp} f$ by the bound $|F(-iy)| \le \|f\|_1 e^{-ay}$. The Phragmén-Lindelöf principle in the lower half plane and the Paley-Wiener theorem show that a smaller rate would move the support to the right of $a$. So $h_F = -a$.

steps.slogan: Show that the growth rates along the imaginary axis add for products.
steps.detail: For entire functions of exponential type that are bounded on the real axis, the limit of $y^{-1}\log|F(-iy)|$ exists, by Jensen's formula and Phragmén-Lindelöf bounds. Limits of logarithms add under products, so $h_{FG} = h_F + h_G$.

steps.slogan: Apply the left-end formula to $F$, $G$ and $F G$.
steps.detail: Step 3 gives $-\inf\operatorname{supp}(f * g) = h_{FG}$, and step 4 gives $h_{FG} = h_F + h_G = -a - b$. So $\inf\operatorname{supp}(f * g) = a + b$ for $f_R, g_R$, and hence for $f, g$ by step 1.

concepts.c:convolution: The theorem describes where the convolution is supported.
concepts.c:support: The left end of the support is the quantity that adds.
concepts.c:fourier-laplace-transform: The transform turns the convolution into a product of entire functions.
concepts.c:entire-function: Growth and zero estimates for entire functions drive the argument.
concepts.c:function-of-exponential-type: Compactly supported integrable functions have transforms of exponential type.

statement: Let $E$ be an [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) over $\mathbb{Q}$ (Mazur's torsion theorem). Then $E(\mathbb{Q})_{\mathrm{tors}}$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/n$ with $1 \le n \le 10$ or $n = 12$, or to $\mathbb{Z}/2 \times \mathbb{Z}/2m$ with $1 \le m \le 4$.

hypotheses.text: $E$ is an [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) defined over $\mathbb{Q}$.

conclusion: The torsion subgroup $E(\mathbb{Q})_{\mathrm{tors}}$ is one of the fifteen groups in the statement.

proofs.name: Eisenstein ideal and formal immersion
proofs.slogan: Turn torsion points into rational points of modular curves, then use the Eisenstein quotient of the Jacobian and a formal immersion to exclude every other group.
proofs.scope: An outline of Mazur's theorem, the case of the torsion conjecture over $\mathbb{Q}$ that the record's alias names. The conjecture for higher dimensional abelian varieties is open and not covered.

roles.why: A rational point of order $N$ on $E$ gives a rational non-cuspidal point of the modular curve $X_1(N)$.

steps.slogan: Turn a rational point of order $N$ into a rational point of $X_1(N)$.
steps.detail: By the moduli interpretation of the [modular curve](c:modular-curve) $X_1(N)$, a pair $(E, P)$ with $P \in E(\mathbb{Q})$ of exact order $N \ge 4$ is a non-cuspidal rational point of $X_1(N)$, and conversely. Groups $\mathbb{Z}/2 \times \mathbb{Z}/2m$ use the analogous curve $X_1(2, 2m)$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the exclusion of all other groups to prime levels and finitely many small cases.
steps.detail: A group outside the list contains a point of prime order $p \ge 11$, or a subgroup from a finite list of small groups. The small cases fall to the Weil pairing or to explicit rational points of modular curves of small genus (Ogg, Kubert, Mazur-Tate). Prime levels $p \ge 11$ are the main case.

steps.slogan: Build the Eisenstein quotient of the Jacobian of $X_0(p)$ and show that it has rank zero.
steps.detail: For prime $p$, Mazur studies the Eisenstein ideal $I$ in the Hecke algebra $\mathbb{T}$ of the [Jacobian](c:jacobian-variety) $J_0(p)$ and the quotient $\tilde{J}$ attached to an Eisenstein prime. He proves that $\tilde{J}(\mathbb{Q})$ is finite. By the Mordell-Weil theorem the group is finitely generated, so finiteness means rank zero and finite torsion.

steps.slogan: Show that $X_0(p)$ embeds formally in $\tilde{J}$ at the cusp.
steps.detail: Mazur proves that the map $X_0(p) \to \tilde{J}$ with the cusp $\infty$ as base point is a formal immersion at $\infty$ at suitable primes. With the structure of the cuspidal and Shimura subgroups, a rational point of the cover $X_1(p)$ must map into the finite group $\tilde{J}(\mathbb{Q})$ in a controlled way.

steps.slogan: Conclude that rational points of order $p \ge 11$ are cuspidal and read off the list.
steps.detail: Finiteness of $\tilde{J}(\mathbb{Q})$ and the formal immersion give: $X_1(p)$ has no non-cuspidal rational point for $p \ge 11$ (for $p = 11, 13$ the curves have genus $1$ and $2$ and their rational points were known earlier). With step 2 no group outside the list occurs.

concepts.c:elliptic-curve: The theorem bounds the torsion of rational points on an elliptic curve.
concepts.c:modular-curve: Torsion points of order $N$ are rational points on the modular curve $X_1(N)$.
concepts.c:jacobian-variety: The Eisenstein quotient is a quotient of the Jacobian of $X_0(p)$.

source.ref: B. Mazur, Modular curves and the Eisenstein ideal, Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS 47 (1977), 33-186
source.note: The steps follow Mazur's paper: modular curves, Eisenstein ideal and quotient, formal immersion, then the cases for prime and composite levels.

statement: Let $d, r \ge 1$ be integers. Any set of at least $(d+1)(r-1)+1$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ can be partitioned into $r$ parts whose [convex hulls](c:convex-hull) have a common point.

hypotheses.text: $d$ and $r$ are positive integers.
$S \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ has at least $N + 1$ points, where $N = (d+1)(r-1)$.

conclusion: There are disjoint sets $P_1, \dots, P_r$ with union $S$ and $\bigcap_{j} \operatorname{conv} P_j \ne \emptyset$.

proofs.name: Sarkaria's tensor trick
proofs.slogan: Lift the points, tensor them with the vertices of a simplex, and apply the colorful Carathéodory theorem to get a colorful choice with zero in its hull.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; points beyond $N + 1$ join any part, since hulls only grow. The case $r = 2$ is Radon's theorem.

roles.why: The number $r$ gives a simplex in $\mathbb{R}^{r-1}$, and $d$ gives the lifted space $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ with $N = (d+1)(r-1)$.
Exactly $N + 1$ points give $N + 1$ color classes, one more than the dimension $N$ of the tensor space.

steps.slogan: Lift the points to height one and fix the vertices of a regular simplex.
steps.detail: Take $x_0, \dots, x_N \in \mathbb{R}^d$ from $S$ and put $y_i = (x_i, 1) \in \mathbb{R}^{d+1}$. Let $v_1, \dots, v_r \in \mathbb{R}^{r-1}$ be the vertices of a regular simplex centered at $0$. Then $\sum_j v_j = 0$, and this is the only linear relation among the $v_j$ up to scalars.

steps.slogan: Form the color classes $C_i = \{y_i \otimes v_j : 1 \le j \le r\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$.
steps.detail: The vectors $y_i \otimes v_j$ lie in $\mathbb{R}^{d+1} \otimes \mathbb{R}^{r-1} = \mathbb{R}^N$, which is the [tensor product](c:tensor-product). There are $N + 1$ classes, and $0 = \frac1r \sum_j y_i \otimes v_j$ lies in $\operatorname{conv} C_i$ for each $i$.

steps.slogan: Apply the colorful Carathéodory theorem to find one vector per class with $0$ in their hull.
steps.detail: Take a transversal $T$ whose hull has nearest point $p \ne 0$ to $0$. By Carathéodory on the hyperplane $\langle x, p\rangle = |p|^2$, $p$ lies in the hull of at most $N$ points of $T$, so some class $C_i$ is unused. A $y \in C_i$ has $\langle y, p \rangle \le 0$, and swapping it in gives a point nearer to $0$ on $[p, y]$. So $p = 0$.

steps.slogan: Read the parts and the weights off the colorful choice.
steps.detail: We get $j(i)$ and $\lambda_i \ge 0$ with $\sum_i \lambda_i = 1$ and $\sum_i \lambda_i\, y_i \otimes v_{j(i)} = 0$. Put $P_j = \{i : j(i) = j\}$, which partition the indices, and $w_j = \sum_{i \in P_j} \lambda_i y_i$. Then $\sum_j w_j \otimes v_j = 0$.

steps.slogan: Use the single relation among the $v_j$ to make all $w_j$ equal.
steps.detail: For each coordinate $k$ of $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ we have $\sum_j w_j^{(k)} v_j = 0$. The only relations among $v_1, \dots, v_r$ are multiples of $\sum_j v_j = 0$, so $w_j^{(k)}$ does not depend on $j$. Hence $w_1 = \cdots = w_r = w$.

steps.slogan: Compare last coordinates to get a common point of the hulls.
steps.detail: The last coordinate of $w_j$ is $\sum_{i \in P_j}\lambda_i$, equal for all $j$ and summing to $1$, so each equals $1/r$. Thus no $P_j$ is empty, and the first $d$ coordinates of $r w$ give $x = \sum_{i \in P_j} r\lambda_i x_i \in \operatorname{conv}\{x_i : i \in P_j\}$ for every $j$.

concepts.c:convex-hull: The hulls of the parts must share a point, which is what the proof builds.
concepts.c:tensor-product: Tensoring lifted points with simplex vertices encodes the partition in one space.

source.note: Sarkaria's tensor trick in the form of I. Bárány and S. Onn, Colourful linear programming and its relatives, Math. Oper. Res. 22 (1997); colorful Carathéodory by I. Bárány, Discrete Math. 40 (1982).
